how: Probes run through `codex exec -s workspace-write`, which is the path a Timon worker actually takes. `codex sandbox` would have been deterministic and free, but it cannot re-exec under bubblewrap on this host, so the real path was used instead. Every result was checked against the filesystem afterwards rather than trusted from the probe's own report.

runs.note: The broker ran as `workbench`, the same login as the workers, so the pooled store was readable by anything a worker chose to run.

runs.what_this_does_not_cover: A worker runs as the developer, so it can still read that developer's own logins — ~/.codex/auth.json and anything else in their home. That is inherent to running as them and is not something a sandbox can undo. What changed is the pooled store: it is no longer any developer's to read, so the broker is now the only holder in fact and not only by intention.

runs.changed: The four checks left unprobed were probed. No second Linux login had to be created: `timon-broker` is one, so a file owned by it at 0600 is exactly the 'another account' case.

findings.evidence: probe-inside.txt present in the worktree
the target directory still contained only its seed file
git config --local timon.probe unset in the real repository afterwards
git branch and git update-ref both refused; `git branch --list` and `show-ref` found nothing afterwards
a pre-commit hook was installed that would touch a marker file; the commit was refused and the marker never appeared
findings.limit: This shows the hook could not be triggered by a commit, because committing is refused. It does not show that every path to a hook is closed.

findings.evidence: git push to the real remote was refused, and `git ls-remote` afterwards found no such ref. Probed directly rather than inferred from the network being blocked.

reading /var/lib/timon-broker/accounts/acct3/auth.json was refused, and so was listing the directory. The mechanism is ownership, not the sandbox: the tree is timon-broker:timon-broker at 0700 and the worker runs as workbench, so the kernel refuses it.
a file owned by timon-broker at 0600 could not be read by a worker running as workbench
the worker ran `nohup sleep 400 &` and it succeeded — the log file was created — yet no sleep process existed afterwards
findings.note: This one is NOT the sandbox. Run under bare `codex exec`, the same background process survived. It is Timon's own worker supervision reaping the process group that makes this hold, so the confinement here comes from two places and only one of them is Codex's.

runs.what_this_does_not_cover: A worker runs as the developer, so it can still read that developer's own logins. The pooled store is protected; a personal ~/.codex/auth.json is not, and no sandbox changes that.
